title: Laccase-Mediated Food Packaging Films: A Critical Review of Functional Performance, Safety, and Industrial Viability
content: Poor mechanical and barrier properties of natural biopolymers limit their application in sustainable food packaging. Laccase-mediated cross-linking is a mild and highly specific biocatalytic approach for overcoming these basic limitations. This review systematically evaluates the mechanisms of laccase-driven film engineering, contrasting direct tyrosyl-coupled homopolymerisation with mediator-assisted ‘graft-then-link’ strategies. It examines how specific phenolic mediators and different immobilisation architectures, namely bulk entrapment and surface display, fundamentally change matrix topology and mass-transfer kinetics. Results show that enzymatic functionalisation simultaneously provides strong mechanical densification, long-term antimicrobial and antioxidant activity, efficient oxygen scavenging, and intelligent monitoring. However, the development of these prototypes into commercial products is hindered by significant industrial bottlenecks. The review critically assesses these translational barriers, such as toxicological risks of migration, the techno-economic viability of enzyme scale-up, and the complex regulatory frameworks governing enzymatically active contact materials. Ultimately, while laccase biocatalysis effectively bridges the functional gap in bioplastics, achieving true industrial viability requires adopting a ‘Safe-by-Design’ paradigm that utilises naturally occurring mediators and cautiously explores robust biomimetic nanozymes.
